items.title: Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations
items.content: At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet. Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance. This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives significant advertiser value and capacity efficiency. Inference fleets face a capacity paradox: They can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta, we built a system that aggregates these pockets into a shared opportunistic capacity pool and turns them into better ads recommendations. By putting otherwise idle capacity to work, the system helps people see more relevant ads and improves advertiser outcomes without requiring additional capacity orders. Using this opportunistic capacity safely is difficult. It’s distributed across team-owned capacity allocations, regions, and accelerator types, and may be reclaimed with little notice. The ads inference system must therefore adapt workload as capacity supply changes without overloading the dedicated capacity that serves baseline workload. We address this challenge with two complementary elasticity levers. Rank More Ads (RMA) adjusts the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages. Serve Better Models (SBM) adjusts the share of requests routed to a more powerful model. Physical and logical isolation protects the capacity reserved for baseline serving. Separate feedback loops control RMA candidate volume and SBM model coverage, while value-aware load shedding at both servers and clients allows the system to degrade gracefully when capacity is suddenly reclaimed. Together, these mechanisms allow optional work to expand and contract with opportunistic capacity while protecting latency and reliability. The Inference Capacity Paradox: Globally Constrained, but Locally Idle Inference fleets must maintain enough capacity to meet demand under strict latency and reliability targets. However, demand and capacity rarely align perfectly across time, regions, resource combinations, and accelerator types. Capacity can therefore remain idle in parts of a fleet even when the fleet is constrained overall. Common causes include: Peak-provisioning and demand-variation mismatch: Inference fleets must be provisioned for peak demand, while traffic varies by time of day and season. Capacity needed during peak periods can therefore remain temporarily idle when demand is lower. Model-development and capacity-delivery timing mismatch: Inference capacity arrives on supply-chain timelines, whereas models are developed and launched on separate schedules. This creates a gap between when capacity becomes available and when models are ready to consume it. Regional resource-ratio mismatch: Inference workloads require accelerators as well as supporting resources such as CPUs. When these resources are not available in the required proportions, one resource can remain idle while another limits serving capacity. Accelerator-type mismatch: Inference fleets can span multiple accelerator vendors, generations, and architectures. Workloads are not always portable across these accelerator types, which can strand capacity on hardware that cannot immediately serve the available demand. These mismatches create an industry-wide inference capacity paradox: A fleet can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta’s scale, these temporary pockets can collectively represent substantial capacity and create better ads recommendations when used safely. From Fragmented Reservations to a Shared Opportunistic Capacity Pool Across a heterogeneous fleet at Meta’s scale, instantaneous idle inference capacity is inevitable — even with proactive planning designed to minimize structural mismatches. However, because this capacity is inherently tied to fluctuating baseline demands, it comes with distinct operational constraints — it’s preemptible (can be reclaimed at any time), highly volatile in its availability, and carries no long-term guarantees. To successfully consume this volatile resource without compromising baseline performance, workloads must exhibit certain structural properties: A high degree of workload elasticity: The workload can quickly add or remove a large amount of optional work as the pool changes without affecting baseline expectations. Sustained quality at scale: The workload can continue to meaningfully improve output quality across the range the opportunistic pool can supply. This type of workload often already uses a large amount of dedicated capacity due to this property. Limited cross-service dependencies: A self-contained workload reduces the number of upstream and downstream systems that must respond to volatile capacity. Two Complementary Elasticity Levers Based on these structural properties, we identified two complementary levers that meet these criteria to consume this idle capacity and generate large value upside. Rank More Ads (RMA) For each user request, the ads recommendation system must select a small number of ads from millions of candidates in less than a second. The system uses a sequence of ranking stages in which increasingly powerful machine learning models evaluate progressively smaller candidate sets. The later stages only evaluate the top candidates from the previous stage. RMA increases the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages when opportunistic capacity is available. Evaluating more candidates increases the chance of finding ads that are relevant to the user. Because the additional candidates pass through CPU-heavy upstream (e.g., retrieval, feature processing) as well as accelerator-heavy inference, RMA generally requires both CPU and accelerator surplus. Serve Better Models (SBM) The ads evaluation can use models with different levels of complexity. More powerful models can improve prediction quality, but it’s not efficient to use them for every request with dedicated capacity. SBM changes the share of requests evaluated by the more powerful models as accelerator capacity changes. It keeps the number of ads entering the ranking stages constant, so upstream CPU demand remains comparatively stable. This allows SBM to use accelerator-only surplus that RMA cannot consume. The SBM model-router component uses request-value signals to prioritize the requests expected to benefit most from a more powerful model. Why Both Levers Are Needed The two levers consume different combinations of resources. RMA requires both CPU and accelerator capacity, while SBM can use accelerator capacity without substantially increasing upstream CPU work. Together, they can use a broader range of opportunistic capacity than either lever alone. The incremental impact of each lever also changes with traffic, current coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates to serve better ads or by routing more requests to a powerful model for improved prediction accuracy. We periodically adjust the allocation between RMA and SBM based on their measured performance and resource requirements. Safely Using Opportunistic Capacity for Ads Inference Opportunistic capacity can be reclaimed faster than the control loops that regulate work across a large serving fleet. We therefore design the system around one requirement – losing opportunistic capacity may reduce incremental ranking work, but it must not overload the capacity that serves the baseline workload. We support this requirement through isolated routing targets, two workload-specific feedback loops, and fast local load shedding. Protecting Baseline Traffic Through Physical and Logical Isolation Optional work must not consume the capacity reserved for baseline serving. SBM and RMA enforce this separation differently. For SBM, the isolation is physical. The baseline and more powerful models use separate routing targets. Dedicated replicas are sized to serve requests with the baseline model, while replicas on opportunistic capacity serve requests selected for the more powerful model. When opportunistic capacity contracts, the system reduces the share of requests routed to the more powerful model. Those requests use the baseline model instead, whose capacity is already provisioned for them. For RMA, the isolation is logical. The system calculates how much additional candidate-ranking work can be supported by the model replicas deployed on opportunistic capacity and uses total capacity to set a global budget for RMA. Each model replica may receive a mixture of baseline and additional work; individual requests do not need to be physically separated. Baseline traffic is protected by limiting the total incremental work to the amount that these replicas can support. When opportunistic capacity contracts, RMA reduces its global candidate-volume target and SBM reduces its more-powerful-model coverage. In both cases, the system removes optional work rather than allowing it to spill onto the capacity reserved for baseline serving. This keeps baseline traffic within its latency and reliability targets. Controlling Candidate Volume With Latency Feedback RMA uses a closed feedback loop composed of a central proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller and client-side enforcement. Looking through a simplified lens, the controller uses observed tail latency to calculate a target for the number of ads sent to downstream ranking, and clients apply that target to new requests. When latency is below the target, the controller increases the number of ads ranked. When latency rises, it reduces the number. This allows RMA to use the latency signal, which is influenced by the capacity situation, to converge on a sustainable candidate volume as conditions change. Routing Requests With Value-Aware Model Selection SBM uses a corresponding feedback loop with central control and client-side routing. The central controller sets the target coverage for the more powerful model, and the client-side model router decides which eligible requests use that model and which continue through the baseline model. The router uses a request-value signal to group requests into segments based on predicted likelihood of user engagement with the ad. An explore-and-exploit process periodically measures the incremental outcome of using the more powerful model in each segment and updates the allocation between the two models. This is necessary because the incremental benefit of the more powerful model does not always align with the absolute value of a request. The process also preserves exploratory traffic across segments so the system continues to collect the observations needed to adapt, rather than reinforcing an outdated routing decision. A calibration loop keeps the realized traffic share close to its target as the traffic mix changes across regions and over time. When capacity contracts, the central controller reduces the target coverage and the client routes fewer requests to the more powerful model. Requests removed from the opportunistic path continue through the baseline model. Multi-Layer Value-Aware Load Shedding The RMA and SBM feedback loops continuously align opportunistic work with available capacity, but their central components operate on the order of minutes. A sudden preemption can therefore remove capacity before clients receive new targets. The system adds value-aware protection for both workloads that can react immediately: Server-side shedding: If the opportunistic pool loses capacity before the clients’ view has caught up, servers immediately remove lower-value opportunistic work. For RMA, they reduce the number of candidates processed within individual requests; SBM applies an equivalent value-aware shedding policy to requests routed to the more powerful model. This absorbs rapid changes close to the serving bottleneck. Client-side shedding: The RMA and SBM clients use the latest controller targets as the guideline but also observe the server status directly. When it’s observed that the server is overloaded, clients shed lower-value opportunistic work directly, i.e., RMA requests fewer additional ads, while SBM routes fewer requests to the more powerful model. Both forms of load shedding react within a few milliseconds, bridging the interval before the controller-client loops converge. Both server-side shedding and client-side shedding use value signals when selecting work to remove, which minimizes the effect during the transition. Current Work and What Comes Next Increasing Workload Elasticity We aim to use more opportunistic capacity productively by extending the operating range of RMA and SBM and broadening the set of elasticity levers. For RMA, this means supporting higher candidate volumes across ranking stages; for SBM, using more powerful models that turn additional accelerator capacity into better predictions. We are also developing new levers such as precomputation elasticity, which performs work ahead of request time and is therefore less constrained by the location and timing of live traffic. Expanding the Usable Capacity Pool Opportunistic capacity is fragmented across regions and accelerator types, and it’s useful only when compatible models and supporting resources are available in the same place. We are expanding model portability and cross-region inference capabilities so that more of the available capacity can be used efficiently. Automating Value-Based Capacity Allocation The incremental impact of each lever changes with traffic, coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates or by routing more requests to a powerful model. We are building an optimization-based system to automatically adjust the allocation of AI inference capacity to its possible elasticity levers based on the benefits to users and advertisers. The goal is to maximize the return of the capacity subject to the constraints that each use case has in terms of regional constraints, hardware compatibility, and durability requirements for the idle capacity, among others. Acknowledgments This work reflects critical contributions from a cross functional v-team across Meta: David Amsallem, Mohit Bharti, Maddie Digne, Stephen Dimmick, Maomao Ding, Amit Dutta, Sebin George, Aashik Gowda, Atul Goyal, Mohak Goyal, Nelson Guo, Tiger Hao, Yaning Huang, Dianshi Li, Yang Li, Bai Liu, Bofeng Liu, Wei Liu, Yisi Liu, Daniel Molina Hurtado, Maciej Naruszewicz, Arka Pal, Annan Pan, Brian Park, Brian Peschka, Michael Shao, Bikash Sharma, Alexander Sun, Weiman Sun, Kaiyue Tao, Patrick Taylor, Kevin Tong, Ellie Wen, Chao Xie, Lu Yang, Sihan You, Hansen Zhang, and Anthony Zhu We also thank the following leaders for their sponsorship and support: Neeraj Agrawal, Justin Charlap, Brian Ellis, Prabhakar Goyal, Hong Jiang, Shri Karandikar, Santanu Kolay, Uladzimir Pashkevich, Rob Schwartzberg, Eric Shan, Matt Steiner, Nathan Yan, Tak Yan, Caijie Zhang, and Alex Zhong The post Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files. Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version. The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content"). items.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
items.author: vishnukool
items.content: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks! https://agent37.com

items.title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase
items.author: Christopher Harrison
items.content: Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types. Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task. In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we’ll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project: Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow. Agent skills package repeatable procedures. Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connect Copilot to external tools and data sources, expanding what it can do. Let’s look at how each one works and how they can work together. Start with custom instructions Suppose you ask Copilot to add a custom page size to an application. Making the change is only part of the job. The new code should also follow the patterns your team already uses. Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation. You can also create path-specific instruction files inside .github/instructions. These files use an applyTo field to tell Copilot when the guidance is relevant. When Copilot works on a matching file, it can use both the repository-wide instructions and the more specific guidance. That lets you keep the broad rules in one place without forcing every file type into the same mold. Package repeatable procedures as agent skills Custom instructions are useful for standards that should shape many tasks. But some guidance only matters when Copilot is performing a particular procedure, such as running quality checks, preparing a release, or debugging a failed workflow. That’s where agent skills come in. A skill is a folder containing instructions and, optionally, scripts and other resources that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Project-level skills can live in .github/skills, with each skill in its own subfolder. For example, a .github/skills/quality-checks folder could contain a SKILL.md file that explains: When Copilot should use the skill. Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting. What each script checks. How to troubleshoot common failures. The description in SKILL.md helps Copilot determine when the skill applies. After updating the interface, Copilot can load the quality-checks skill and follow the project’s established process for testing and linting instead of guessing which commands to run. Use a custom agent for broader, specialized work Some tasks are larger than a single procedure. An accessibility review, for example, may require Copilot to inspect components, templates, styles, and interactions across multiple files. Custom agents let you create specialized versions of Copilot for work like this. A repository-level agent profile lives in .github/agents and can define the agent’s purpose, instructions, tools, and relevant project context. Use a custom agent when a recurring type of work benefits from a dedicated role or perspective, especially when the task may span multiple files and draw on several tools or sources of context. Connect Copilot to external tools with MCP servers Instructions, skills, and agents help Copilot understand how to work within your project. MCP servers expand what it can access and do beyond the repository. MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, and services. A documentation server can give it access to framework guidance, while a server such as Playwright can let it open and interact with your application in a browser. You can browse available MCP servers in the Copilot app or add a custom one. Once Playwright is configured, you can ask: Use the Playwright MCP server to test the functionality manually. Copilot can then use Playwright to open the application in a browser and interact with it much as you would. That gives it a way to verify not only that the code passes automated checks, but also that the updated interface behaves as expected. Choose the right type of customizations These customizations solve different problems, but they become more useful when you combine them: Custom instructions define the conventions Copilot should follow across the repository or for particular files. Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Custom agents provide focused expertise and guidance for broader tasks. MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, services, and data sources, expanding what Copilot can do. Take this with you Giving Copilot useful project context starts with four questions: What project convention do I keep explaining? What multi-step procedure do I repeat? What complex task could benefit from a dedicated custom agent? What outside tool or source does Copilot need? Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made instructions, skills, agents, and more through Awesome Copilot. Find one that addresses a workflow you already repeat, review what it contains, and adapt it to your repository’s tools and standards. Start small: choose one convention you keep explaining, add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md, and see how Copilot applies it to your next task. items.title: Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: When Russia began attacking Ukrainian data centers and telecommunication infrastructure, it apparently failed to prepare for possible retaliation. Now Russia’s digital services are facing widespread outages after Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of the largest data centers owned by Russian tech giant Yandex within several days. items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.content: Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation: lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]] [*L for L in lists] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}] {*s for s in sets} # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}] {**d for d in dicts} # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling. Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported. My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc. Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system. I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. Tags: open-source, profiling, python, sqlite, uv

items.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.content: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today. The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows. Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factory The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud. Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work. Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days. To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48. “I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.” From agent rosters to dynamic workflows The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents. “Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.” The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Image via Anthropic Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work. “Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said. That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish. “It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said. All of this is available in Claude Console, the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents. Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located. The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern: a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts, and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report. Q&A: Budgets and the limits of self-improvement The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs, and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents? “The answer really is evals and lower defaults,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization. One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget. Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available? Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience. Scanner in the stock watchlist example. A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time? Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming. In the documentation, “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store,” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.” Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.” For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run? Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop. The brain/hands conceptual overview of Managed Agents. What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents, another audience member asked. Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console. “You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent? You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.” Another interesting question was whether the subagents can communicate with each other? Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API. Flows cost much more, but are designed for big tasks In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.” Setting a budget is key! The bigger question is how ambitious can flows be, really? One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem. While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too. “Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, broadly doable by the general public.”

items.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police
items.author: Jon Brodkin
items.content: An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, the company and police department confirmed on Friday. A Claude model sent the false tip on July 18 to the Philadelphia Police Department's website for submitting information about unsolved murders, but it was flagged by a spam filter. Anthropic apparently discovered the incident on September 28 and informed the police department about it on October 8. During internal testing, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete various forms up to the final submission stage and to stop before submitting those forms. "Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page," Anthropic said in a report describing "unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude." items.title: WHO report on Russian lab worker death highlights "key uncertainty"
items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that "key uncertainty," the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease. The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. "However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure," the agency wrote in its report. The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8. Read full article Comments

items.title: OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
items.content: At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube). Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol. Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP. We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure. At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative. This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone. Here’s some of what’s new: The 102.4T scale-out switch: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters. The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across for multi-site clusters: Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips. Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA): a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations. The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack. IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers. The IcePack rack — Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack, populated with IceCube 102T switch blades. IceCube — Meta’s 102.4 Tbps liquid-cooled switch blade, delivering 128×800G non-blocking capacity and running FBOSS. Scaling AI Fabrics From Building to Region As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): More Resilient, Larger Clusters We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric. With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages: Larger non-blocking GPU clusters compared to single-plane topologies, which enables the scale required for our largest AI training workloads A flattened topology, moving from the 3-tier Clos fabric of our NSF fabric to a 2-tier Clos fabric. Removing this tier of switches reduces network hops, latency, and infrastructure cost. NIC-level hardware load balancing: Load balancing, traditionally done by network switches, now starts at the NIC, which sprays every packet across all eight planes in hardware. A combined control plane for fault tolerance: The control plane of FPF includes both the switches and the hosts, allowing the host to steer traffic away from downed planes. Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings. Bridging On-Prem Data Centers and Public Cloud This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure. Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit. That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale. At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches. The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work. BAG: Scale-Across Aggregation The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space. At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement. Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff. We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG. The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors. Backend aggregation (BAG) connects building-scale AI fabrics — both DSF and NSF — across sub-regions into a unified training network. SRv6-Powered Regional Backbone Using FBOSS We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI. Meta’s Regional Backbone (RBB) interconnects data center campuses and bridges to public cloud capacity. Ethernet for Scale-Up: Our Commitment to Ethernet A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies. Tahan: Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology. Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS. Tahan, Meta’s first open, Ethernet-based scale-up switch (32×800G), liquid-cooled and running FBOSS. Next-Generation Scale-Up: 72 Accelerators per Rack on 102.4T Silicon We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack. The next-generation MTIA scale-up blade: 216×400G on 102.4 Tbps silicon, adopting OCP ESUN as the scale-up data plane. ESUN Evolving The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for: Protocol headers and framing optimized for scale-up topologies. Error handling mechanisms for lossless multi-hop fabrics. Alignment with UEC and IEEE standards. This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it. Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases. ESUN’s technical focus: a fabric-centric scope that preserves GPU implementation flexibility, coordinated with IEEE and UEC standards work with the ESUN 1.0 specification already released. With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future. Ecosystem Enablement and Open Transport Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols. OSPA: Open Switch Platform Architecture SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable. To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer. OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for: Power management and power sequencing. Sensor and environment control, including thermal and fan management. Hardware inventory management and device enumeration. Out-of-band hardware interfaces (management Ethernet, serial console, USB, LED indicators). Firmware maintenance and updates. Platform troubleshooting and diagnostics. FBOSS Ecosystem Enablement Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware. Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository. MetaRoCE: Open-Source Transport for AI Clusters As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics. At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack. Join Us in Building the Open Future of AI Networking The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone. We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands. The authors are members of the Network Infrastructure team at Meta. items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April. The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman's death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state's health department. In an emailed statement to The Washington Post, the coroner's office said the primary cause of death was listed as "probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles."
